[61911] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 tit. 2 And it seems not.

[61912] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 1 For it is called Ecclesi. 15, 18: before man life and death, good and evil: whatsoever he will, it shall be given him. From this it may be understood that sin, which is the spiritual death of the soul, consists in the will. But nothing that man contracts from his origin consists in his will. Therefore man contracts no sin from his origin.

[61913] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 2 Further, an accident is not translated except by the translation of its subject. But the subject of sin is the rational soul. Since, then, the rational soul is not translated by origin, as we find in Lib. of Eccl. dogmas, it seems that no sin is contracted by origin.

[61914] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 3 But it must be said that although the subject of sin is not translated, the flesh is nevertheless translated, which is the cause of sin. because when they are placed, no effect is placed. But the flesh is not a sufficient cause of sin; for no matter how much the flesh entices to sin, it is still in the power of the will to consent or not to consent; and thus the will itself is a sufficient cause of sin. But the will is not translated. Therefore the transfer of the flesh is not sufficient for the transfer of any sin.

[61915] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 4 Further, sin, as it is now accepted, is to whom punishment and rebuke are due. But no rebuke and punishment is due to any defect contracted from the origin: for as the Philosopher says in Ethic. but he is reprimanded if he is blind from drunkenness. Therefore no defect which is contracted from the origin has the character of sin.

[61916] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 5 Further, Augustine distinguishes two kinds of evil in 1 On free will: one that we do, which is the evil of guilt, and another that we suffer, which belongs to the evil of punishment. But every deficiency which is from another has the aspect of suffering; for passion is the effect and inference of action. Therefore nothing contracted by origin from another has the character of sin, but only the character of punishment.

[61917] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 6 Further, in Lib. It is said of ecclesiastical dogmas: Our flesh is good, since it was created by a good God. But good is not the cause of evil, according to Matt. 7, 18: a tree cannot produce good fruit that is bad. Therefore original sin is not contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61918] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 7 Further, the soul depends more on the flesh after it is united to it than on its union itself. But after the soul is already united to the flesh, it cannot be infected by the flesh except by its consent. Therefore, neither in the union itself. Therefore original sin cannot be contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61919] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Objection 8. Further, if a vitiated origin of the flesh causes sin in the soul, the more vitiated by its origin, the greater the sin it will cause. But in those who are born of fornication, the origin is more defective than in those who are born of legitimate marriage. It would therefore follow that those who are born from fornication contract a greater sin by being born; which is evidently false: because no greater punishment is due to them.

[61920] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, if original sin is contracted through the origin of the flesh, this is only in so far as the flesh is corrupted. Then that corruption is either moral or natural. But it cannot be moral: because the subject of moral corruption is not the flesh, but the soul. Similarly, neither is the natural: because it follows that it infects the soul with natural activity, that is, through active and passive qualities; which is clearly false. In no way, therefore, is sin contracted through the origin of the flesh.

[61921] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 10 Further, the defect which resulted from the sin of the first parent is the lack of original justice, as Anselm says; and so since the original justice is something spiritual, it follows that the aforesaid deficiency is also spiritual. But the corruption of the flesh is something corporeal. But the spiritual and the corporeal are of different kinds; and thus the spiritual cannot cause a bodily effect. Therefore, the corruption in our flesh could not have been caused by the sin of the first parent, from which sin was transfused into us through the origin.

[61922] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, according to Augustine, original sin is the lack of original justice. Either then the original justice belonged to the soul of the first man naturally from his own creation, or it was an added gift from divine liberality. But if it had been a natural soul, it would never have lost it by sinning: because, as Dionysius says, chapter 4. of Div. Nom., natural data also remained in the demons; and thus also all men would have original justice: because what is natural to one soul is natural to all souls; and thus no one would be born with original sin, that is, with a lack of original righteousness. But if that justice was a gift added from divine liberality: then either God gives that gift to the soul of man being born, or not. If he gives, man is not born with a lack of original justice, nor can his soul be infected by the flesh. But if it is not given by God, this does not seem to be imputed to him, but to God, who did not give. In no way, therefore, can man contract original sin.

[61923] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 12 Further, the rational soul does not come upon any pre-existing form: because it does not come to matter as a substantial form, but as accidental matter, which comes to a subject already existing in act. It is necessary, therefore, that when the rational soul arrives, all pre-existing forms should fail, and consequently all accidents. Therefore the corruption of the seed also ceases, if it was inherent in the progenitor. Therefore the coming soul cannot be defiled by the flesh.

[61924] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 13 Further, motion follows the nature of the predominant element in mixed bodies, and consequently all the properties result from that which predominates in the compound. But the soul predominates over the body in man, which is composed of both; but the soul has purity from its origin. Although, therefore, the flesh has contracted some impurity from its origin, it seems that a person who is born should not be said to be infected with sin, but pure.

[61925] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 14. Further, there is a sin to which some punishment is due: but a sin which is contracted through the origin, no punishment is due; for the lack of divine vision, which is commonly assigned to him as a punishment, does not seem to be any kind of punishment; because if a man died without all sin, and had no grace, he would not be able to reach the divine vision, in which eternal life consists, according to John 17, v. 3: this is eternal life, that they may know you alone as the true God; and the Apostle says, Rom. 6, 23: eternal life by the grace of God. Therefore there is no sin which is contracted by origin.

[61926] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, just as the first cause is more noble than the second, so the second cause is more noble than the effect. But if sin is transmitted from the first parent, corruption has followed in the flesh through the soul of the first man who sinned, and it is brought from the flesh to the soul of the man who is born from Adam; and thus the soul of the first man is like the first cause, and the flesh like the second cause, and the soul of the man begotten like the last effect. Thus, then, the soul of the first man will be more noble, and the flesh more noble than the soul of the first man; which is inappropriate. Therefore, sin cannot be transmitted by origin.

[61927] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 16 Further, he does nothing except in so far as he actually is. But there is no actual sin in the seed. Therefore, the soul cannot be infected with any sin through the seed that has been cut.

[61928] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 17 Further, the cause of the infection of sin and merit cannot be the same. But the act of generation can sometimes be meritorious; for example, when a man existing in grace goes to his wife for the purpose of begetting children, or to repay a debt. Therefore the infection of sin in the offspring cannot be caused from this.

[61929] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 18 Further, a particular cause does not bring about a universal effect. But Adam's sin was a particular one. Therefore he could not infect the whole human nature with any sin.

[61930] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 19 Further, the Lord says Ezek. 18, v. 4: All souls are mine; and verse 30: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. But it would bear, if for the sin of the first man those who are born from him were condemned. Therefore sin is not transferred to Adam's descendants because of her sin.

[61931] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 1 Sed contra. Est quod dicitur, Rom. V, v. 12: through one man sin entered into this world. Sed non per imitationem; because thus sin entered the world through the Devil, according to Wisdom. II, 24-25: the envy of the Devil, death entered the world. Let those who are from his side imitate him. Therefore, through a vitiated origin, sin is derived from the first man to posterity.

[61932] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. Objection 2. Further, Augustine says in Chapter 14 of the City of God that the first man, being depraved of his own accord, begat depraved children. But perversion does not take place except through sin. Therefore the children of Adam contract sin from their origin.

[61933] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 co. I answer It must be said that the Pelagians denied that any sin could be transmitted through origin. But this to a great extent excludes the necessity of the redemption effected by Christ, which seems to have been most necessary to abolish the infection of sin, which was derived from the first parent into all his posterity, as the apostle says, Rom. 5:18, that just as by the offense of one there is a process on all men to condemnation, so also by the righteousness of one on all men to the justification of life. The necessity of baptizing children is also excluded, which is nevertheless a common custom of the Church derived from the apostles, as Dionysius says in the Ecclesiastical Hierar. And therefore it must be said simply that sin is transmitted by origin from the first parent to the posterity. For the evidence of which we must consider that a singular person can be considered in two ways: in the first way, according to the fact that he is a certain singular person; in another way, according to the fact that it is a part of some college, and in both ways an act may belong to it. For it belongs to him in so far as he is a singular person, that act which he does of his own free will and by himself; but in so far as he is a part of the college, any act which he does not do by himself or of his own free will, but which is done by the whole college, or by several of the college, or by the leader of the college, may belong to him. just as what the ruler of the state does, the state is said to do, as the philosopher says. For such a college of men is regarded as one man, so that different men are appointed to different offices as if they were different members of one natural body, as the Apostle says about the members of the Church, 1 Cor. 12, 12. Thus, therefore, the whole multitude of men who receive human nature from their first parent, is to be considered as one college, or rather as one body of one man; in which multitude each man, even Adam himself, may be considered either as a singular person, or as some member of this multitude, which is derived by natural origin from one. Now it must be considered that the first man, in his institution, had been divinely given a certain supernatural gift, namely, original justice, by which reason was subject to God, and the lower powers of reason, and the body of the soul. Now this gift had not been given to the first man as a singular person only, but as a certain principle of the whole human nature, namely, that it should be derived from him through the origin to posterity. But this gift received by the first man, by sinning through his free will, he lost in the manner in which it had been given to him, that is, for himself and for all his posterity. Therefore, the failure of this gift affects all his posterity; and thus this defect is transmitted to posterity in the same way as human nature is transmitted; which indeed is translated not according to itself as a whole, but according to some part of itself, that is, according to the flesh, into which God infuses the soul; and thus, just as the divinely infused soul belongs to the human nature derived from Adam, because of the flesh to which it is united; so also the aforesaid defect pertains to the soul because of the flesh, which is propagated from Adam not only according to the corpulent substance, but also according to the seminal reason, that is, not only materially, but as from an active principle: for thus the son receives from the father the human nature. If, therefore, this defect is considered to have been derived in this way by origin in that man, according to the fact that this man is a kind of singular person, then this kind of defect cannot have the character of guilt, for the character of which it is required that it be voluntary. But if this man begotten be considered as a certain member of the whole human nature propagated by the first parent, as if all men were one man, then he has the reason of guilt because of his voluntary principle, which is the actual sin of the first parent. as if we were to say that the movement of the hand to commit murder, according as the hand is considered by itself, has no reason for guilt, because the hand is necessarily moved by another. But if it be considered that he is a part of the whole man, who acts by his will, he has the reason of guilt, because he is thus voluntary. Just as, then, murder is not called the fault of the hand, but the fault of the whole man; Thus a deficiency of this kind is not said to be a personal sin, but a sin of the whole nature. nor does it pertain to the person, except in so far as nature infects the person. And just as different parts of man are used to commit one sin, namely the will, the reason, the hands, and the like, and yet there is only one sin because of the unity of the principle, namely the will, from which the reason for sin is derived for all the acts of the parts. so also by reason of the principle in all human nature it is considered as one original sin; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; which, according to Augustine, can be understood in which namely the first man, or in which sin of the first man, so that the sin of the first man is as it were the common sin of all.

[61934] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 1 To the first reply, therefore, that a sin which is contracted by origin is said to be voluntary by reason of its principle, namely, the will of the first parent, as has been said.

[61935] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 2 To the second reply, that this sin follows the whole human nature; whence the subject of this sin is the soul, inasmuch as it is a part of human nature: and therefore as human nature is transgressed, although the soul is not transgressed; so even original sin is transferred, although the soul is not transferred.

[61936] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 3 Reply to Objection 3: The flesh is not a sufficient cause of actual sin, but it is a sufficient cause of original sin. just as the transmigration of the flesh is a sufficient cause, however materially, of human nature.

[61937] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 4 Reply to the fourth, that what is contracted by origin is not due punishment and rebuke if it is referred to a person, because in this way it does not have the aspect of the will, but if it is related to nature, it has the aspect of the will, as has been said, and in this way rebuke and punishment are due to it.

[61938] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 5. To the fifth answer, that a deficiency by the origin of a contract indeed has the aspect of existing from another, if it is referred to a person, but not if it is referred to a nature. for it is so, as it were, from an intrinsic principle.

[61939] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 6. To the sixth answer, that our flesh is good in its own nature, but inasmuch as it is deprived of original justice because of the sin of the first parent, so it causes original sin.

[61940] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 7. To the seventh answer, that, as has been said, original sin, speaking in itself, is a sin of the nature, not of the person, but by reason of the infected nature. Now the act of generation properly serves nature, because it is directed to the preservation of the species; but the fact that the flesh is already united to the soul belongs to the constitution of the person; and therefore the flesh causes original sin more as it is considered in the way of generation than as it is already united.

[61941] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 8. To the eighth answer, that in those who are born of fornication, it is indeed twofold in origin, viz., the vice of nature, which is transmitted from Adam, and the vice of the person, that is, the begetting father, from which vice no infection is left in the offspring. For everyone who begets transmits original sin to the extent that he generates like Adam, not to the extent that he generates like Peter or Martin; that is by what he has from Adam, not by what is proper to him.

[61942] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 9. To the ninth answer, that the corruption which is in the flesh is indeed a natural act, but by intention and moral virtue. For from the sin of the first parent his flesh was deprived of that virtue, so that from it the seed may be dropped by which the original righteousness is propagated to others; and thus in the seed the lack of this virtue is the lack of moral corruption, and a kind of intention thereof; as we say that the concentration of color is in the air, and the concentration of the soul is in the seed. And from this also there is virtue for a similar imperfection, just as there is virtue for the production of human nature in offspring.

[61943] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 10. To answer the tenth, that nothing prevents a spiritual cause from causing a corporeal effect. For Boethius also says in his book on the Trinity that the forms which are in matter came from the forms which are without matter: and in us the lower appetite is moved by the will, to the movement of which bodily transformation follows.

[61944] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 11 Regarding the eleventh answer, that the original justice was added to the first man out of divine liberality; but what is not given to this soul by God is not on his part, but on the part of human nature, in which the contrary is found preventing.

[61945] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 12. Regarding the twelfth answer, that the corruption of original sin is in the seed, not actually but by virtue, in the same way that human nature is there by virtue: which virtue is active in the seed in the foaming spirit, as Aristotle says in Lib. of Gen. of animals, but not in matter which loses one form and receives another.

[61946] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 13 Regarding the thirteenth point, as Dionysius says in chapter 4. of Div. Nom., good occurs from a whole whole cause, but evil also results from individual defects; and therefore the deficiency which is in the part of the body is sufficient to take away the integrity of human nature.

[61947] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 14. To the fourteenth answer, that the lack of divine vision befits a person in two ways. On the one hand, this is because he does not have in himself the means by which he can reach the divine vision, and thus the lack of divine vision would belong to him who was in the natural sun even without sin. for thus the lack of the divine vision is not a punishment, but a deficiency consequent upon all created nature: for no creature of its natural nature can attain to the divine vision. In another way, the lack of divine vision may belong to someone in this way, that he has something in himself from which it is due to him that he lacks divine vision; and thus the lack of divine vision is the punishment of both original and actual sin.

[61948] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 15 The fifteenth point is that the cause is twofold. One of the principal things that acts through its own form, and this is more noble than the effect in so far as it is the cause. There is another instrumental cause which does not act through its own form, but in so far as it is moved by another, and this need not be more noble in its effect, just as a saw is not more noble than a house. But in this way the carnal seed is the cause of the human nature in the offspring, and also of the original guilt in his soul.

[61949] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 16 To answer the sixteenth, that any agent is in act in many ways. In the first way, according to the proper form, which either contains the form of the effect according to the likeness of the species, just as fire begets fire; or according to power only, as the sun generates fire. In another way, according to motion from another; and in this way the instrument acts as an actual being: and so also the seed is actually, in so far as there is in it the movement and intention of the generative soul, according to the philosopher in Lib. of Gen. of animals; and from this he has the power of causing both human nature and original sin.

[61950] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 17 To the seventeenth answer, that a man, by approaching his wife justly, deserves according to what is proper to him; and so he does not transmit original sin, but according to what he has from Adam, as was said above.

[61951] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 18. To answer the eighteenth, that Adam, in so far as he was the principle of human nature, had the idea of a universal cause, and thus by his act the whole of human nature, which is propagated by him, was corrupted.

[61952] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 19 To answer the nineteenth, that the sin of the first man is in a way the common sin of the whole human nature, as has been said; and therefore when a man is punished for the sin of his first parent, he is not punished for the sin of another, but for his own sin.
en.text: [61911] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 tit. 2 And it seems not. [61912] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 1 For it is called Ecclesi. 15, 18: before man life and death, good and evil: whatsoever he will, it shall be given him. From this it may be understood that sin, which is the spiritual death of the soul, consists in the will. But nothing that man contracts from his origin consists in his will. Therefore man contracts no sin from his origin. [61913] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 2 Further, an accident is not translated except by the translation of its subject. But the subject of sin is the rational soul. Since, then, the rational soul is not translated by origin, as we find in Lib. of Eccl. dogmas, it seems that no sin is contracted by origin. [61914] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 3 But it must be said that although the subject of sin is not translated, the flesh is nevertheless translated, which is the cause of sin. because when they are placed, no effect is placed. But the flesh is not a sufficient cause of sin; for no matter how much the flesh entices to sin, it is still in the power of the will to consent or not to consent; and thus the will itself is a sufficient cause of sin. But the will is not translated. Therefore the transfer of the flesh is not sufficient for the transfer of any sin. [61915] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 4 Further, sin, as it is now accepted, is to whom punishment and rebuke are due. But no rebuke and punishment is due to any defect contracted from the origin: for as the Philosopher says in Ethic. but he is reprimanded if he is blind from drunkenness. Therefore no defect which is contracted from the origin has the character of sin. [61916] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 5 Further, Augustine distinguishes two kinds of evil in 1 On free will: one that we do, which is the evil of guilt, and another that we suffer, which belongs to the evil of punishment. But every deficiency which is from another has the aspect of suffering; for passion is the effect and inference of action. Therefore nothing contracted by origin from another has the character of sin, but only the character of punishment. [61917] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 6 Further, in Lib. It is said of ecclesiastical dogmas: Our flesh is good, since it was created by a good God. But good is not the cause of evil, according to Matt. 7, 18: a tree cannot produce good fruit that is bad. Therefore original sin is not contracted through the origin of the flesh. [61918] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 7 Further, the soul depends more on the flesh after it is united to it than on its union itself. But after the soul is already united to the flesh, it cannot be infected by the flesh except by its consent. Therefore, neither in the union itself. Therefore original sin cannot be contracted through the origin of the flesh. [61919] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Objection 8. Further, if a vitiated origin of the flesh causes sin in the soul, the more vitiated by its origin, the greater the sin it will cause. But in those who are born of fornication, the origin is more defective than in those who are born of legitimate marriage. It would therefore follow that those who are born from fornication contract a greater sin by being born; which is evidently false: because no greater punishment is due to them. [61920] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, if original sin is contracted through the origin of the flesh, this is only in so far as the flesh is corrupted. Then that corruption is either moral or natural. But it cannot be moral: because the subject of moral corruption is not the flesh, but the soul. Similarly, neither is the natural: because it follows that it infects the soul with natural activity, that is, through active and passive qualities; which is clearly false. In no way, therefore, is sin contracted through the origin of the flesh. [61921] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 10 Further, the defect which resulted from the sin of the first parent is the lack of original justice, as Anselm says; and so since the original justice is something spiritual, it follows that the aforesaid deficiency is also spiritual. But the corruption of the flesh is something corporeal. But the spiritual and the corporeal are of different kinds; and thus the spiritual cannot cause a bodily effect. Therefore, the corruption in our flesh could not have been caused by the sin of the first parent, from which sin was transfused into us through the origin. [61922] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, according to Augustine, original sin is the lack of original justice. Either then the original justice belonged to the soul of the first man naturally from his own creation, or it was an added gift from divine liberality. But if it had been a natural soul, it would never have lost it by sinning: because, as Dionysius says, chapter 4. of Div. Nom., natural data also remained in the demons; and thus also all men would have original justice: because what is natural to one soul is natural to all souls; and thus no one would be born with original sin, that is, with a lack of original righteousness. But if that justice was a gift added from divine liberality: then either God gives that gift to the soul of man being born, or not. If he gives, man is not born with a lack of original justice, nor can his soul be infected by the flesh. But if it is not given by God, this does not seem to be imputed to him, but to God, who did not give. In no way, therefore, can man contract original sin. [61923] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 12 Further, the rational soul does not come upon any pre-existing form: because it does not come to matter as a substantial form, but as accidental matter, which comes to a subject already existing in act. It is necessary, therefore, that when the rational soul arrives, all pre-existing forms should fail, and consequently all accidents. Therefore the corruption of the seed also ceases, if it was inherent in the progenitor. Therefore the coming soul cannot be defiled by the flesh. [61924] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 13 Further, motion follows the nature of the predominant element in mixed bodies, and consequently all the properties result from that which predominates in the compound. But the soul predominates over the body in man, which is composed of both; but the soul has purity from its origin. Although, therefore, the flesh has contracted some impurity from its origin, it seems that a person who is born should not be said to be infected with sin, but pure. [61925] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 14. Further, there is a sin to which some punishment is due: but a sin which is contracted through the origin, no punishment is due; for the lack of divine vision, which is commonly assigned to him as a punishment, does not seem to be any kind of punishment; because if a man died without all sin, and had no grace, he would not be able to reach the divine vision, in which eternal life consists, according to John 17, v. 3: this is eternal life, that they may know you alone as the true God; and the Apostle says, Rom. 6, 23: eternal life by the grace of God. Therefore there is no sin which is contracted by origin. [61926] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. Further, just as the first cause is more noble than the second, so the second cause is more noble than the effect. But if sin is transmitted from the first parent, corruption has followed in the flesh through the soul of the first man who sinned, and it is brought from the flesh to the soul of the man who is born from Adam; and thus the soul of the first man is like the first cause, and the flesh like the second cause, and the soul of the man begotten like the last effect. Thus, then, the soul of the first man will be more noble, and the flesh more noble than the soul of the first man; which is inappropriate. Therefore, sin cannot be transmitted by origin. [61927] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 16 Further, he does nothing except in so far as he actually is. But there is no actual sin in the seed. Therefore, the soul cannot be infected with any sin through the seed that has been cut. [61928] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 17 Further, the cause of the infection of sin and merit cannot be the same. But the act of generation can sometimes be meritorious; for example, when a man existing in grace goes to his wife for the purpose of begetting children, or to repay a debt. Therefore the infection of sin in the offspring cannot be caused from this. [61929] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 18 Further, a particular cause does not bring about a universal effect. But Adam's sin was a particular one. Therefore he could not infect the whole human nature with any sin. [61930] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 arg. 19 Further, the Lord says Ezek. 18, v. 4: All souls are mine; and verse 30: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. But it would bear, if for the sin of the first man those who are born from him were condemned. Therefore sin is not transferred to Adam's descendants because of her sin. [61931] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. 1 Sed contra. Est quod dicitur, Rom. V, v. 12: through one man sin entered into this world. Sed non per imitationem; because thus sin entered the world through the Devil, according to Wisdom. II, 24-25: the envy of the Devil, death entered the world. Let those who are from his side imitate him. Therefore, through a vitiated origin, sin is derived from the first man to posterity. [61932] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 s. c. Objection 2. Further, Augustine says in Chapter 14 of the City of God that the first man, being depraved of his own accord, begat depraved children. But perversion does not take place except through sin. Therefore the children of Adam contract sin from their origin. [61933] De malo, q. 4 a. 1 co. I answer It must be said that the Pelagians denied that any sin could be transmitted through origin. But this to a great extent excludes the necessity of the redemption effected by Christ, which seems to have been most necessary to abolish the infection of sin, which was derived from the first parent into all his posterity, as the apostle says, Rom. 5:18, that just as by the offense of one there is a process on all men to condemnation, so also by the righteousness of one on all men to the justification of life. The necessity of baptizing children is also excluded, which is nevertheless a common custom of the Church derived from the apostles, as Dionysius says in the Ecclesiastical Hierar. And therefore it must be said simply that sin is transmitted by origin from the first parent to the posterity. For the evidence of which we must consider that a singular person can be considered in two ways: in the first way, according to the fact that he is a certain singular person; in another way, according to the fact that it is a part of some college, and in both ways an act may belong to it. For it belongs to him in so far as he is a singular person, that act which he does of his own free will and by himself; but in so far as he is a part of the college, any act which he does not do by himself or of his own free will, but which is done by the whole college, or by several of the college, or by the leader of the college, may belong to him. just as what the ruler of the state does, the state is said to do, as the philosopher says. For such a college of men is regarded as one man, so that different men are appointed to different offices as if they were different members of one natural body, as the Apostle says about the members of the Church, 1 Cor. 12, 12. Thus, therefore, the whole multitude of men who receive human nature from their first parent, is to be considered as one college, or rather as one body of one man; in which multitude each man, even Adam himself, may be considered either as a singular person, or as some member of this multitude, which is derived by natural origin from one. Now it must be considered that the first man, in his institution, had been divinely given a certain supernatural gift, namely, original justice, by which reason was subject to God, and the lower powers of reason, and the body of the soul. Now this gift had not been given to the first man as a singular person only, but as a certain principle of the whole human nature, namely, that it should be derived from him through the origin to posterity. But this gift received by the first man, by sinning through his free will, he lost in the manner in which it had been given to him, that is, for himself and for all his posterity. Therefore, the failure of this gift affects all his posterity; and thus this defect is transmitted to posterity in the same way as human nature is transmitted; which indeed is translated not according to itself as a whole, but according to some part of itself, that is, according to the flesh, into which God infuses the soul; and thus, just as the divinely infused soul belongs to the human nature derived from Adam, because of the flesh to which it is united; so also the aforesaid defect pertains to the soul because of the flesh, which is propagated from Adam not only according to the corpulent substance, but also according to the seminal reason, that is, not only materially, but as from an active principle: for thus the son receives from the father the human nature. If, therefore, this defect is considered to have been derived in this way by origin in that man, according to the fact that this man is a kind of singular person, then this kind of defect cannot have the character of guilt, for the character of which it is required that it be voluntary. But if this man begotten be considered as a certain member of the whole human nature propagated by the first parent, as if all men were one man, then he has the reason of guilt because of his voluntary principle, which is the actual sin of the first parent. as if we were to say that the movement of the hand to commit murder, according as the hand is considered by itself, has no reason for guilt, because the hand is necessarily moved by another. But if it be considered that he is a part of the whole man, who acts by his will, he has the reason of guilt, because he is thus voluntary. Just as, then, murder is not called the fault of the hand, but the fault of the whole man; Thus a deficiency of this kind is not said to be a personal sin, but a sin of the whole nature. nor does it pertain to the person, except in so far as nature infects the person. And just as different parts of man are used to commit one sin, namely the will, the reason, the hands, and the like, and yet there is only one sin because of the unity of the principle, namely the will, from which the reason for sin is derived for all the acts of the parts. so also by reason of the principle in all human nature it is considered as one original sin; propter quod apostolus dicit, Rom. V, 12: in quo omnes peccaverunt; which, according to Augustine, can be understood in which namely the first man, or in which sin of the first man, so that the sin of the first man is as it were the common sin of all. [61934] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 1 To the first reply, therefore, that a sin which is contracted by origin is said to be voluntary by reason of its principle, namely, the will of the first parent, as has been said. [61935] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 2 To the second reply, that this sin follows the whole human nature; whence the subject of this sin is the soul, inasmuch as it is a part of human nature: and therefore as human nature is transgressed, although the soul is not transgressed; so even original sin is transferred, although the soul is not transferred. [61936] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 3 Reply to Objection 3: The flesh is not a sufficient cause of actual sin, but it is a sufficient cause of original sin. just as the transmigration of the flesh is a sufficient cause, however materially, of human nature. [61937] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 4 Reply to the fourth, that what is contracted by origin is not due punishment and rebuke if it is referred to a person, because in this way it does not have the aspect of the will, but if it is related to nature, it has the aspect of the will, as has been said, and in this way rebuke and punishment are due to it. [61938] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 5. To the fifth answer, that a deficiency by the origin of a contract indeed has the aspect of existing from another, if it is referred to a person, but not if it is referred to a nature. for it is so, as it were, from an intrinsic principle. [61939] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 6. To the sixth answer, that our flesh is good in its own nature, but inasmuch as it is deprived of original justice because of the sin of the first parent, so it causes original sin. [61940] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 7. To the seventh answer, that, as has been said, original sin, speaking in itself, is a sin of the nature, not of the person, but by reason of the infected nature. Now the act of generation properly serves nature, because it is directed to the preservation of the species; but the fact that the flesh is already united to the soul belongs to the constitution of the person; and therefore the flesh causes original sin more as it is considered in the way of generation than as it is already united. [61941] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 8. To the eighth answer, that in those who are born of fornication, it is indeed twofold in origin, viz., the vice of nature, which is transmitted from Adam, and the vice of the person, that is, the begetting father, from which vice no infection is left in the offspring. For everyone who begets transmits original sin to the extent that he generates like Adam, not to the extent that he generates like Peter or Martin; that is by what he has from Adam, not by what is proper to him. [61942] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 9. To the ninth answer, that the corruption which is in the flesh is indeed a natural act, but by intention and moral virtue. For from the sin of the first parent his flesh was deprived of that virtue, so that from it the seed may be dropped by which the original righteousness is propagated to others; and thus in the seed the lack of this virtue is the lack of moral corruption, and a kind of intention thereof; as we say that the concentration of color is in the air, and the concentration of the soul is in the seed. And from this also there is virtue for a similar imperfection, just as there is virtue for the production of human nature in offspring. [61943] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 10. To answer the tenth, that nothing prevents a spiritual cause from causing a corporeal effect. For Boethius also says in his book on the Trinity that the forms which are in matter came from the forms which are without matter: and in us the lower appetite is moved by the will, to the movement of which bodily transformation follows. [61944] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 11 Regarding the eleventh answer, that the original justice was added to the first man out of divine liberality; but what is not given to this soul by God is not on his part, but on the part of human nature, in which the contrary is found preventing. [61945] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 12. Regarding the twelfth answer, that the corruption of original sin is in the seed, not actually but by virtue, in the same way that human nature is there by virtue: which virtue is active in the seed in the foaming spirit, as Aristotle says in Lib. of Gen. of animals, but not in matter which loses one form and receives another. [61946] Of evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 13 Regarding the thirteenth point, as Dionysius says in chapter 4. of Div. Nom., good occurs from a whole whole cause, but evil also results from individual defects; and therefore the deficiency which is in the part of the body is sufficient to take away the integrity of human nature. [61947] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 14. To the fourteenth answer, that the lack of divine vision befits a person in two ways. On the one hand, this is because he does not have in himself the means by which he can reach the divine vision, and thus the lack of divine vision would belong to him who was in the natural sun even without sin. for thus the lack of the divine vision is not a punishment, but a deficiency consequent upon all created nature: for no creature of its natural nature can attain to the divine vision. In another way, the lack of divine vision may belong to someone in this way, that he has something in himself from which it is due to him that he lacks divine vision; and thus the lack of divine vision is the punishment of both original and actual sin. [61948] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 15 The fifteenth point is that the cause is twofold. One of the principal things that acts through its own form, and this is more noble than the effect in so far as it is the cause. There is another instrumental cause which does not act through its own form, but in so far as it is moved by another, and this need not be more noble in its effect, just as a saw is not more noble than a house. But in this way the carnal seed is the cause of the human nature in the offspring, and also of the original guilt in his soul. [61949] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 16 To answer the sixteenth, that any agent is in act in many ways. In the first way, according to the proper form, which either contains the form of the effect according to the likeness of the species, just as fire begets fire; or according to power only, as the sun generates fire. In another way, according to motion from another; and in this way the instrument acts as an actual being: and so also the seed is actually, in so far as there is in it the movement and intention of the generative soul, according to the philosopher in Lib. of Gen. of animals; and from this he has the power of causing both human nature and original sin. [61950] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 17 To the seventeenth answer, that a man, by approaching his wife justly, deserves according to what is proper to him; and so he does not transmit original sin, but according to what he has from Adam, as was said above. [61951] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 18. To answer the eighteenth, that Adam, in so far as he was the principle of human nature, had the idea of a universal cause, and thus by his act the whole of human nature, which is propagated by him, was corrupted. [61952] On evil, q. 4 a. 1 to 19 To answer the nineteenth, that the sin of the first man is in a way the common sin of the whole human nature, as has been said; and therefore when a man is punished for the sin of his first parent, he is not punished for the sin of another, but for his own sin.

document:aquinas-sth:iii-51-3.title: St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae
document:aquinas-sth:iii-51-3.translationNote: Open-source bilingual Latin and English text.
document:aquinas-sth:iii-51-3.contentHtml:
Latin

Ad tertium sic proceditur. Videtur quod corpus Christi in sepulcro fuerit incineratum. Sicut enim mors est poena peccati primi parentis, ita etiam incineratio, dictum est enim primo homini post peccatum, pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris, ut dicitur Gen. III. Sed Christus mortem sustinuit ut nos a morte liberaret. Ergo etiam incinerari debuit corpus eius, ut nos ab incineratione liberaret.

Praeterea, corpus Christi fuit eiusdem naturae cum corporibus nostris. Sed corpora nostra statim post mortem resolvi incipiunt et ad putrefactionem disponuntur, quia, exhalante calido naturali, supervenit calor extraneus, qui putrefactionem causat. Ergo videtur quod similiter in corpore Christi acciderit.

Praeterea, sicut dictum est, Christus sepeliri voluit ut daret hominibus spem resurgendi etiam de sepulcris. Ergo etiam incinerationem pati debuit, ut spem resurgendi incineratis post incinerationem daret.

Sed contra est quod in Psalmo dicitur, non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem, quod Damascenus exponit, in III libro, de corruptione quae est per resolutionem in elementa.

Respondeo dicendum quod non fuit conveniens corpus Christi putrefieri, vel quocumque modo incinerari. Quia putrefactio cuiuscumque corporis provenit ex infirmitate naturae illius corporis, quae non potest amplius corpus continere in unum. Mors autem Christi, sicut supra dictum est, non debuit esse cum infirmitate naturae, ne crederetur non esse voluntaria. Et ideo non ex morbo, sed ex passione illata voluit mori, cui se obtulit sponte. Et ideo Christus, ne mors eius naturae infirmitati adscriberetur, noluit corpus suum qualitercumque putrefieri, aut qualitercumque resolvi, sed, ad ostensionem virtutis divinae, voluit corpus illud incorruptum permanere. Unde Chrysostomus dicit quod, viventibus aliis hominibus, his scilicet qui egerunt strenue, arrident propria gesta, his autem pereuntibus, pereunt. Sed in Christo est totum contrarium, nam ante crucem, omnia sunt maesta et infirma; ut autem crucifixus est, omnia clariora sunt facta, ut noscas non purum hominem crucifixum.

Ad primum ergo dicendum quod Christus, cum non esset subiectus peccato, neque morti erat obnoxius neque incinerationi. Voluntarie tamen mortem sustinuit propter nostram salutem, propter rationes supra dictas. Si autem corpus eius fuisset putrefactum vel resolutum, magis hoc fuisset in detrimentum humanae salutis, dum non crederetur in eo esse virtus divina. Unde ex persona eius in Psalmo dicitur, quae utilitas in sanguine meo dum descendo in corruptionem? Quasi dicat, si corpus meum putrescat, perdetur effusi sanguinis utilitas.

Ad secundum dicendum quod corpus Christi, quantum ad conditionem naturae passibilis, putrefactibile fuit, licet non quantum ad meritum putrefactionis, quod est peccatum. Sed virtus divina corpus Christi a putrefactione reservavit, sicut et resuscitavit a morte.

Ad tertium dicendum quod Christus de sepulcro resurrexit virtute divina, quae nullis terminis coarctatur. Et ideo hoc quod a sepulcro surrexit, sufficiens argumentum fuit quod homines erant resuscitandi virtute divina non solum de sepulcris, sed etiam de quibuscumque cineribus.

English

Objection 1: It would seem that Christ's body was reduced to dust in the tomb. For just as man dies in punishment of his first parent's sin, so also does he return to dust, since it was said to the first man after his sin: "Dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return" (Gn. 3:19). But Christ endured death in order to deliver us from death. Therefore His body ought to be made to return to dust, so as to free us from the same penalty.

Objection 2: Further, Christ's body was of the same nature as ours. But directly after death our bodies begin to dissolve into dust, and are disposed towards putrefaction, because when the natural heat departs, there supervenes heat from without which causes corruption. Therefore it seems that the same thing happened to Christ's body.

Objection 3: Further, as stated above (Article [1]), Christ willed to be buried in order to furnish men with the hope of rising likewise from the grave. Consequently, He sought likewise to return to dust so as to give to them who have returned to dust the hope of rising from the dust.

On the contrary, It is written (Ps. 15:10): "Nor wilt Thou suffer Thy holy one to see corruption": and Damascene (De Fide Orth. iii) expounds this of the corruption which comes of dissolving into elements.

I answer that, It was not fitting for Christ's body to putrefy, or in any way be reduced to dust, since the putrefaction of any body comes of that body's infirmity of nature, which can no longer hold the body together. But as was said above (Question [50], Article [1], ad 2), Christ's death ought not to come from weakness of nature, lest it might not be believed to be voluntary: and therefore He willed to die, not from sickness, but from suffering inflicted on Him, to which He gave Himself up willingly. And therefore, lest His death might be ascribed to infirmity of nature, Christ did not wish His body to putrefy in any way or dissolve no matter how; but for the manifestation of His Divine power He willed that His body should continue incorrupt. Hence Chrysostom says (Cont. Jud. et Gent. quod 'Christus sit Deus') that "with other men, especially with such as have wrought strenuously, their deeds shine forth in their lifetime; but as soon as they die, their deeds go with them. But it is quite the contrary with Christ: because previous to the cross all is sadness and weakness, but as soon as He is crucified, everything comes to light, in order that you may learn it was not an ordinary man that was crucified."

Reply to Objection 1: Since Christ was not subject to sin, neither was He prone to die or to return to dust. Yet of His own will He endured death for our salvation, for the reasons alleged above (Question [51], Article [1]). But had His body putrefied or dissolved, this fact would have been detrimental to man's salvation, for it would not have seemed credible that the Divine power was in Him. Hence it is on His behalf that it is written (Ps. 19:10): "What profit is there in my blood, whilst I go down to corruption?" as if He were to say: "If My body corrupt, the profit of the blood shed will be lost."

Reply to Objection 2: Christ's body was a subject of corruption according to the condition of its passible nature, but not as to the deserving cause of putrefaction, which is sin: but the Divine power preserved Christ's body from putrefying, just as it raised it up from death.

Reply to Objection 3: Christ rose from the tomb by Divine power, which is not narrowed within bounds. Consequently, His rising from the grave was a sufficient argument to prove that men are to be raised up by Divine power, not only from their graves, but also from any dust whatever.

Sed contra est quod in Psalmo dicitur, non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem, quod Damascenus exponit, in III libro, de corruptione quae est per resolutionem in elementa. Respondeo dicendum quod non fuit conveniens corpus Christi putrefieri, vel quocumque modo incinerari. Quia putrefactio cuiuscumque corporis provenit ex infirmitate naturae illius corporis, quae non potest amplius corpus continere in unum. Mors autem Christi, sicut supra dictum est, non debuit esse cum infirmitate naturae, ne crederetur non esse voluntaria. Et ideo non ex morbo, sed ex passione illata voluit mori, cui se obtulit sponte. Et ideo Christus, ne mors eius naturae infirmitati adscriberetur, noluit corpus suum qualitercumque putrefieri, aut qualitercumque resolvi, sed, ad ostensionem virtutis divinae, voluit corpus illud incorruptum permanere. Unde Chrysostomus dicit quod, viventibus aliis hominibus, his scilicet qui egerunt strenue, arrident propria gesta, his autem pereuntibus, pereunt. Sed in Christo est totum contrarium, nam ante crucem, omnia sunt maesta et infirma; ut autem crucifixus est, omnia clariora sunt facta, ut noscas non purum hominem crucifixum. Voluntarie tamen mortem sustinuit propter nostram salutem, propter rationes supra dictas. Si autem corpus eius fuisset putrefactum vel resolutum, magis hoc fuisset in detrimentum humanae salutis, dum non crederetur in eo esse virtus divina. Unde ex persona eius in Psalmo dicitur, quae utilitas in sanguine meo dum descendo in corruptionem? Quasi dicat, si corpus meum putrescat, perdetur effusi sanguinis utilitas. Ad secundum dicendum quod corpus Christi, quantum ad conditionem naturae passibilis, putrefactibile fuit, licet non quantum ad meritum putrefactionis, quod est peccatum. Sed virtus divina corpus Christi a putrefactione reservavit, sicut et resuscitavit a morte. Ad tertium dicendum quod Christus de sepulcro resurrexit virtute divina, quae nullis terminis coarctatur. Et ideo hoc quod a sepulcro surrexit, sufficiens argumentum fuit quod homines erant resuscitandi virtute divina non solum de sepulcris, sed etiam de quibuscumque cineribus. Objection 1: It would seem that Christ's body was reduced to dust in the tomb. For just as man dies in punishment of his first parent's sin, so also does he return to dust, since it was said to the first man after his sin: "Dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return" (Gn. 3:19). But Christ endured death in order to deliver us from death. Therefore His body ought to be made to return to dust, so as to free us from the same penalty. Objection 2: Further, Christ's body was of the same nature as ours. But directly after death our bodies begin to dissolve into dust, and are disposed towards putrefaction, because when the natural heat departs, there supervenes heat from without which causes corruption. Therefore it seems that the same thing happened to Christ's body. Objection 3: Further, as stated above (Article [1]), Christ willed to be buried in order to furnish men with the hope of rising likewise from the grave. Consequently, He sought likewise to return to dust so as to give to them who have returned to dust the hope of rising from the dust. On the contrary, It is written (Ps. 15:10): "Nor wilt Thou suffer Thy holy one to see corruption": and Damascene (De Fide Orth. iii) expounds this of the corruption which comes of dissolving into elements. I answer that, It was not fitting for Christ's body to putrefy, or in any way be reduced to dust, since the putrefaction of any body comes of that body's infirmity of nature, which can no longer hold the body together. But as was said above (Question [50], Article [1], ad 2), Christ's death ought not to come from weakness of nature, lest it might not be believed to be voluntary: and therefore He willed to die, not from sickness, but from suffering inflicted on Him, to which He gave Himself up willingly. And therefore, lest His death might be ascribed to infirmity of nature, Christ did not wish His body to putrefy in any way or dissolve no matter how; but for the manifestation of His Divine power He willed that His body should continue incorrupt. Hence Chrysostom says (Cont. Jud. et Gent. quod 'Christus sit Deus') that "with other men, especially with such as have wrought strenuously, their deeds shine forth in their lifetime; but as soon as they die, their deeds go with them. But it is quite the contrary with Christ: because previous to the cross all is sadness and weakness, but as soon as He is crucified, everything comes to light, in order that you may learn it was not an ordinary man that was crucified." Reply to Objection 1: Since Christ was not subject to sin, neither was He prone to die or to return to dust. Yet of His own will He endured death for our salvation, for the reasons alleged above (Question [51], Article [1]). But had His body putrefied or dissolved, this fact would have been detrimental to man's salvation, for it would not have seemed credible that the Divine power was in Him. Hence it is on His behalf that it is written (Ps. 19:10): "What profit is there in my blood, whilst I go down to corruption?" as if He were to say: "If My body corrupt, the profit of the blood shed will be lost." Reply to Objection 2: Christ's body was a subject of corruption according to the condition of its passible nature, but not as to the deserving cause of putrefaction, which is sin: but the Divine power preserved Christ's body from putrefying, just as it raised it up from death. Reply to Objection 3: Christ rose from the tomb by Divine power, which is not narrowed within bounds. Consequently, His rising from the grave was a sufficient argument to prove that men are to be raised up by Divine power, not only from their graves, but also from any dust whatever.

document:aquinas-sth:iii-64-2-ad-3.contentHtml:
Latin

Ad tertium dicendum quod apostoli, et eorum successores, sunt vicarii Dei quantum ad regimen Ecclesiae institutae per fidem et fidei sacramenta. Unde, sicut non licet eis constituere aliam Ecclesiam, ita non licet eis tradere aliam fidem, neque instituere alia sacramenta, sed per sacramenta quae de latere Christi pendentis in cruce fluxerunt, dicitur esse fabricata Ecclesia Christi.

English

Reply to Objection 3: The apostles and their successors are God's vicars in governing the Church which is built on faith and the sacraments of faith. Wherefore, just as they may not institute another Church, so neither may they deliver another faith, nor institute other sacraments: on the contrary, the Church is said to be built up with the sacraments "which flowed from the side of Christ while hanging on the Cross."

document:aquinas-sth:iii-65-3.contentHtml:
Latin

Ad tertium sic proceditur. Videtur quod sacramentum Eucharistiae non sit potissimum inter sacramenta. Bonum enim commune potius est quam bonum unius, ut dicitur I Ethic. Sed matrimonium ordinatur ad bonum commune speciei humanae per viam generationis, sacramentum autem Eucharistiae ordinatur ad bonum proprium sumentis. Ergo non est potissimum sacramentorum.

Praeterea, digniora sacramenta esse videntur quae per maiorem ministrum conferuntur. Sed sacramentum confirmationis et sacramentum ordinis non conferuntur nisi per episcopum, qui est maior minister quam simplex minister, qui est sacerdos, per quem confertur Eucharistiae sacramentum. Ergo illa sacramenta sunt potiora.

Praeterea, sacramenta tanto sunt potiora quanto maiorem virtutem habent. Sed quaedam sacramenta imprimunt characterem, scilicet Baptismus, confirmatio et ordo, quod non facit Eucharistia. Ergo illa sacramenta sunt potiora.

Praeterea, illud videtur esse potius ex quo alia dependent et non e converso. Sed ex Baptismo dependet Eucharistia, non enim potest aliquis Eucharistiam accipere nisi fuerit baptizatus. Ergo Baptismus est potior Eucharistia.

Sed contra est quod Dionysius dicit, III cap. Eccles. Hier., quod non contingit aliquem perfici perfectione hierarchica nisi per divinissimam Eucharistiam. Ergo hoc sacramentum potissimum et perfectivum est omnium aliorum.

Respondeo dicendum quod, simpliciter loquendo, sacramentum Eucharistiae est potissimum inter alia sacramenta. Quod quidem tripliciter apparet. Primo quidem, ex eo quod in eo continetur ipse Christus substantialiter, in aliis autem sacramentis continetur quaedam virtus instrumentalis participata a Christo, ut ex supra dictis patet. Semper autem quod est per essentiam, potius est eo quod est per participationem.

Secundo hoc apparet ex ordine sacramentorum ad invicem, nam omnia alia sacramenta ordinari videntur ad hoc sacramentum sicut ad finem. Manifestum est enim quod sacramentum ordinis ordinatur ad Eucharistiae consecrationem. Sacramentum vero Baptismi ordinatur ad Eucharistiae receptionem. In quo etiam perficitur aliquis per confirmationem, ut non vereatur se subtrahere a tali sacramento. Per poenitentiam etiam et extremam unctionem praeparatur homo ad digne sumendum corpus Christi. Matrimonium autem saltem sua significatione attingit hoc sacramentum, inquantum significat coniunctionem Christi et Ecclesiae, cuius unitas per sacramentum Eucharistiae figuratur, unde et apostolus dicit, Ephes. V, sacramentum hoc magnum est, ego autem dico in Christo et in Ecclesia.

Tertio hoc apparet ex ritu sacramentorum. Nam fere omnia sacramenta in Eucharistia consummantur, ut dicit Dionysius, III cap. Eccles. Hier., sicut patet quod ordinati communicant, et etiam baptizati si sint adulti.

Aliorum autem sacramentorum comparatio ad invicem potest esse multipliciter. Nam in via necessitatis, Baptismus est potissimum sacramentorum; in via autem perfectionis, sacramentum ordinis; medio autem modo se habet sacramentum confirmationis. Sacramentum vero poenitentiae et extremae unctionis sunt inferioris gradus a praedictis sacramentis, quia, sicut dictum est, ordinantur ad vitam Christianam non per se, sed quasi per accidens, scilicet in remedium supervenientis defectus. Inter quae tamen extrema unctio comparatur ad poenitentiam sicut confirmatio ad Baptismum, ita scilicet quod poenitentia est maioris necessitatis, sed extrema unctio est maioris perfectionis.

Ad primum ergo dicendum quod matrimonium ordinatur ad bonum commune corporaliter. Sed bonum commune spirituale totius Ecclesiae continetur substantialiter in ipso Eucharistiae sacramento.

Ad secundum dicendum quod per ordinem et confirmationem deputantur fideles Christi ad aliqua specialia officia, quod pertinet ad officium principis. Et ideo tradere huiusmodi sacramenta pertinet ad solum episcopum, qui est quasi princeps in Ecclesia. Per sacramentum vero Eucharistiae non deputatur homo ad aliquod officium, sed magis hoc sacramentum est finis omnium officiorum, ut dictum est.

Ad tertium dicendum quod character sacramentalis, sicut supra dictum est, quaedam participatio est sacerdotii Christi. Unde sacramentum quod ipsum Christum coniungit homini, est dignius sacramento quod imprimit Christi characterem.

Ad quartum dicendum quod ratio illa procedit ex parte necessitatis. Sic enim Baptismus, cum sit maximae necessitatis, est potissimum sacramentorum. Sicut ordo et confirmatio habent quandam excellentiam ratione ministerii; et matrimonium ratione significationis. Nihil enim prohibet aliquid esse secundum quid dignius, quod tamen non est dignius simpliciter.

English

Objection 1: It seems that the Eucharist is not the principal of the sacraments. For the common good is of more account than the good of the individual (1 Ethic. ii). But Matrimony is ordained to the common good of the human race by means of generation: whereas the sacrament of the Eucharist is ordained to the private good of the recipient. Therefore it is not the greatest of the sacraments.

Objection 2: Further, those sacraments, seemingly, are greater, which are conferred by a greater minister. But the sacraments of Confirmation and order are conferred by a bishop only, who is a greater minister than a mere minister such as a priest, by whom the sacraments of the Eucharist is conferred. Therefore those sacraments are greater.

Objection 3: Further, those sacraments are greater that have the greater power. But some of the sacraments imprint a character, viz. Baptism, Confirmation and order; whereas the Eucharist does not. Therefore those sacraments are greater.

Objection 4: Further, that seems to be greater, on which others depend without its depending on them. But the Eucharist depends on Baptism: since no one can receive the Eucharist except he has been baptized. Therefore Baptism is greater than the Eucharist.

On the contrary, Dionysius says (Eccl. Hier. iii) that "No one receives hierarchical perfection save by the most God-like Eucharist." Therefore this sacrament is greater than all the others and perfects them.

I answer that, Absolutely speaking, the sacrament of the Eucharist is the greatest of all the sacraments: and this may be shown in three ways. First of all because it contains Christ Himself substantially: whereas the other sacraments contain a certain instrumental power which is a share of Christ's power, as we have shown above (Question [62], Article [4], ad 3, Article [5]). Now that which is essentially such is always of more account than that which is such by participation.

Secondly, this is made clear by considering the relation of the sacraments to one another. For all the other sacraments seem to be ordained to this one as to their end. For it is manifest that the sacrament of order is ordained to the consecration of the Eucharist: and the sacrament of Baptism to the reception of the Eucharist: while a man is perfected by Confirmation, so as not to fear to abstain from this sacrament. By Penance and Extreme Unction man is prepared to receive the Body of Christ worthily. And Matrimony at least in its signification, touches this sacrament; in so far as it signifies the union of Christ with the Church, of which union the Eucharist is a figure: hence the Apostle says (Eph. 5:32): "This is a great sacrament: but I speak in Christ and in the Church."

Thirdly, this is made clear by considering the rites of the sacraments. For nearly all the sacraments terminate in the Eucharist, as Dionysius says (Eccl. Hier. iii): thus those who have been ordained receive Holy Communion, as also do those who have been baptized, if they be adults.

The remaining sacraments may be compared to one another in several ways. For on the ground of necessity, Baptism is the greatest of the sacraments; while from the point of view of perfection, order comes first; while Confirmation holds a middle place. The sacraments of Penance and Extreme Unction are on a degree inferior to those mentioned above; because, as stated above (Article [2]), they are ordained to the Christian life, not directly, but accidentally, as it were, that is to say, as remedies against supervening defects. And among these, Extreme Unction is compared to Penance, as Confirmation to Baptism; in such a way, that Penance is more necessary, whereas Extreme Unction is more perfect.

Reply to Objection 1: Matrimony is ordained to the common good as regards the body. But the common spiritual good of the whole Church is contained substantially in the sacrament itself of the Eucharist.

Reply to Objection 2: By order and Confirmation the faithful of Christ are deputed to certain special duties; and this can be done by the prince alone. Consequently the conferring of these sacraments belongs exclusively to a bishop, who is, as it were, a prince in the Church. But a man is not deputed to any duty by the sacrament of the Eucharist, rather is this sacrament the end of all duties, as stated above.

For thus Baptism, being of the greatest necessity, is the greatest of the sacraments, just as order and Confirmation have a certain excellence considered in their administration; and Matrimony by reason of its signification. For there is no reason why a thing should not be greater from a certain point of view which is not greater absolutely speaking.

Therefore those sacraments are greater. Objection 3: Further, those sacraments are greater that have the greater power. But some of the sacraments imprint a character, viz. Baptism, Confirmation and order; whereas the Eucharist does not. Therefore those sacraments are greater. Objection 4: Further, that seems to be greater, on which others depend without its depending on them. But the Eucharist depends on Baptism: since no one can receive the Eucharist except he has been baptized. Therefore Baptism is greater than the Eucharist. On the contrary, Dionysius says (Eccl. Hier. iii) that "No one receives hierarchical perfection save by the most God-like Eucharist." Therefore this sacrament is greater than all the others and perfects them. I answer that, Absolutely speaking, the sacrament of the Eucharist is the greatest of all the sacraments: and this may be shown in three ways. First of all because it contains Christ Himself substantially: whereas the other sacraments contain a certain instrumental power which is a share of Christ's power, as we have shown above (Question [62], Article [4], ad 3, Article [5]). Now that which is essentially such is always of more account than that which is such by participation. Secondly, this is made clear by considering the relation of the sacraments to one another. For all the other sacraments seem to be ordained to this one as to their end. For it is manifest that the sacrament of order is ordained to the consecration of the Eucharist: and the sacrament of Baptism to the reception of the Eucharist: while a man is perfected by Confirmation, so as not to fear to abstain from this sacrament. By Penance and Extreme Unction man is prepared to receive the Body of Christ worthily. And Matrimony at least in its signification, touches this sacrament; in so far as it signifies the union of Christ with the Church, of which union the Eucharist is a figure: hence the Apostle says (Eph. 5:32): "This is a great sacrament: but I speak in Christ and in the Church." Thirdly, this is made clear by considering the rites of the sacraments. For nearly all the sacraments terminate in the Eucharist, as Dionysius says (Eccl. Hier. iii): thus those who have been ordained receive Holy Communion, as also do those who have been baptized, if they be adults. The remaining sacraments may be compared to one another in several ways. For on the ground of necessity, Baptism is the greatest of the sacraments; while from the point of view of perfection, order comes first; while Confirmation holds a middle place. The sacraments of Penance and Extreme Unction are on a degree inferior to those mentioned above; because, as stated above (Article [2]), they are ordained to the Christian life, not directly, but accidentally, as it were, that is to say, as remedies against supervening defects. And among these, Extreme Unction is compared to Penance, as Confirmation to Baptism; in such a way, that Penance is more necessary, whereas Extreme Unction is more perfect. Reply to Objection 1: Matrimony is ordained to the common good as regards the body. But the common spiritual good of the whole Church is contained substantially in the sacrament itself of the Eucharist. Reply to Objection 2: By order and Confirmation the faithful of Christ are deputed to certain special duties; and this can be done by the prince alone. Consequently the conferring of these sacraments belongs exclusively to a bishop, who is, as it were, a prince in the Church. But a man is not deputed to any duty by the sacrament of the Eucharist, rather is this sacrament the end of all duties, as stated above. Reply to Objection 3: The sacramental character, as stated above (Question [63], Article [3]), is a kind of participation in Christ's priesthood. Wherefore the sacrament that unites man to Christ Himself, is greater than a sacrament that imprints Christ's character. Reply to Objection 4: This argument proceeds on the ground of necessity. For thus Baptism, being of the greatest necessity, is the greatest of the sacraments, just as order and Confirmation have a certain excellence considered in their administration; and Matrimony by reason of its signification. For there is no reason why a thing should not be greater from a certain point of view which is not greater absolutely speaking.
